articles.title: Pip assessments need 'fundamental overhaul', report to say
articles.summary: Disability Minister Sir Stephen Timms says he will recommend major reforms to the personal independence payment.
articles.body:
A review into the personal independence payment (Pip) will call for a "fundamental overhaul" of the assessment process to "better recognise people's varying costs and needs", the disability minister has said.

Sir Stephen Timms has been looking into disability benefits in England and Wales for the past year and found the set up was "no longer fit for purpose".

Writing in the Times , he said his review, to be published on Tuesday, would recommend people with the most severe conditions have a "fast track" process which is "less burdensome".

It comes after a separate review into young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) recommended Pip be scrapped and replaced for under-25s.

Sir Stephen, who produced his report alongside disability groups, carers, clinicians and MPs, said that while Pip had the "right aims" when it was created, there have been "marked shifts in the nature of disability and ill health" in the 13 years since.

He said there had been "substantial growth in claims for mental health and neurodiverse conditions as well as changes to wider society and the workplace".

"For those with the most severe conditions and end of life care, the review recommends a fast track which is less burdensome, with assessment capacity freed up for other cases.

"Where claimants do not have additional costs or care needs, we should be signposting them to services and support."

He added: "Someone with a lifelong or degenerative illness should not need regular reassessments which feel adversarial and unnecessary.

"Disabled people must have the chance to participate fully in everyday life, including in work, and need a more personalised, flexible system that supports them to do so, rather than itself being a barrier."

The Timms review was commissioned after a U-turn from former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's government on a plan for major benefit reform in an attempt to reduce the welfare bill by £5bn a year.

More than 130 MPs, including 120 from Labour, signed an amendment to reject plans to cut disability and sickness-related benefit payments in 2025.

The rebels said they opposed the plans because of the number of people expected to be pushed into relative poverty and a lack of consultation at the time.

Disability benefit not fit for purpose, minister leading review says

Number of people claiming key disability benefit hits record high

'Complete system reset' needed to get 440,000 young people into work, says major review

Sir Stephen's long-awaited review comes only a week after a former Labour Health Secretary Alan Milburn handed down his proposed reforms to tackle youth unemployment .

The government welcomed the Milburn review, which included a recommendation to move those aged 18 to 24 off Pip and the health element of universal credit, and onto an entirely new benefits system.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he thought the "same philosophy" could be applied "right through the age range".

At this stage it is unclear how both of the reviews will complement one another.

No 10 has said the government would consider the Timms review "alongside Milburn's and respond in the coming weeks".

The cost of Pip is expected to rise to more than £41bn by 2030, up from £15bn in 2020. It was being claimed by 4m people in the UK as of 30 April 2026, according to the Department for Work and Pensions.

Though reforming the benefit has frequently been looked at as a way to reduce the Treasury's welfare bill, disability charities have described it as a lifeline for many.

Ahead of the Timms review being handed down, disability equality charity Scope said ministers must ensure Pip is not weakened.

"Life costs more when you're disabled, whether you work or not," executive director James Taylor said, adding that Pip was "vital financial support".

"We know there is real fear among disabled people that changes could leave them unable to afford the essentials."

The disability benefit system is devolved in Scotland and will not change in line with England and Wales; however the Timms Review could impact the funding the Scottish government receives.

Disability benefits are also devolved in Northern Ireland, but in practice it reflects any changes made to the system in England and Wales.

articles.title: A Kentucky health-care fraud defendant owing $3.77 million in restitution tried to stop the $2.4 million sale of a company-owned building; a November 20 federal appeals court dismissed his challenges before closing
articles.summary: A Kentucky man's attempt to prevent the sale of a commercial property linked to his health-care fraud case has been rejected by a federal appeals court.
articles.body: A Kentucky man's attempt to prevent the sale of a commercial property linked to his health-care fraud case has been rejected by a federal appeals court. Timothy Ehn, who owes more than $3.77 million in court-ordered restitution, wanted to stop a $2.4 million transaction involving a building owned by a company in which he previously held a 50% stake.The US Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit dismissed three appeals filed by Ehn on Friday. According to the ruling, judges found that he had missed the deadline for challenging the sale approval. They also ruled that his subsequent bankruptcy filing had affected his legal right to contest decisions involving the company's assets.The property, located at 8780 US 42 in Florence, Kentucky, belongs to GT Enterprise LLC. It was the company's primary asset and had been put up for sale during efforts to recover money owed by Ehn and another defendant, William Siefert.The sale was approved by a federal district court on September 16 for $2.4 million. The transaction was scheduled to close on November 23. Ehn approached the appeals court seeking to prevent the deal from going ahead while his legal challenges remained unresolved.How property came under court-appointed receiverThe dispute traces back to a health-care fraud case in which a jury found Ehn and Siefert guilty. Their sentences included financial restitution orders. Ehn was directed to pay $3,773,569.30, while Siefert was ordered to pay $1,968,763.10.The government subsequently sought to recover these amounts by placing liens on the defendants' ownership interests in GT Enterprise. Both men owned half of the company.The district court approved the government's request and appointed Michael B Baker to oversee GT Enterprise and its assets. The receiver was given responsibility for handling the company's property and was allowed to arrange its sale, provided the court approved the transaction.The receiver later approached the district court with a proposal to sell the Florence property for $2.4 million. The court accepted the proposal on September 16.Ehn objected to the steps taken during the receivership proceedings. Once the sale received court approval, he sought to prevent the money generated by the transaction from being distributed. He also wanted the transfer of ownership and other steps connected with the deal stopped.The district court refused to grant his request. Ehn then took the dispute to the Sixth Circuit, asking it to intervene before the scheduled closing.Why appeals court rejected his first challengeOne of Ehn's challenges concerned the district court's decision to approve the sale. However, the appeals court found that he had waited too long to formally contest that order.The applicable deadline in a criminal case is 14 days from the date of the order being challenged. Since the property sale received approval on September 16, Ehn needed to file his appeal within that period. His formal notice of appeal was filed only on November 9.Ehn argued that a motion he had submitted on September 21 should count as an earlier notice of appeal. That application had sought replacement legal representation, more time and protection of the receivership's records and assets.The judges did not accept this argument. They found that the September application did not clearly identify the decision being challenged or specify the court where the appeal was intended to be heard. It therefore did not meet the requirements for a valid notice of appeal.Ehn also disputed the use of the 14-day deadline. He argued that since the government was recovering restitution through a civil process, the longer 60-day appeal period should apply.The court rejected this distinction. It said the underlying case remained criminal, making the 14-day deadline applicable. His November filing was consequently too late for the court to consider his challenge to the sale approval.Bankruptcy left Ehn without right to second appealThe timing of Ehn's bankruptcy filing created a separate problem for his attempt to stop the transaction. He had filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy on September 16, the same day the district court approved the sale. In his bankruptcy proceedings, he listed his 50% ownership interest in GT Enterprise among his assets.The appeals court explained that this interest became part of his bankruptcy estate when he filed the petition. Under Chapter 7 proceedings, a trustee takes control of the debtor's non-exempt assets and handles matters concerning the estate.This meant Ehn could no longer independently pursue claims relating to his former ownership interest in GT Enterprise. The bankruptcy trustee was the person legally entitled to take action on matters affecting that interest.The trustee, however, had not appealed the district court's refusal to halt the property sale. Ehn could not file an appeal using the trustee's rights, the judges said.Ehn had also argued that the commercial property itself did not belong to his bankruptcy estate. The court said this did not resolve the issue because the relevant asset was his stake in GT Enterprise.That ownership interest had already become part of the bankruptcy estate. The court therefore found that Ehn could not demonstrate the legal standing required to challenge the order refusing to stop the sale.Court dismisses all three appealsThe Sixth Circuit concluded that it could not hear Ehn's challenges. His appeal against the sale approval was filed outside the permitted period, while his challenge to the refusal to halt the transaction failed because he no longer had the necessary legal standing.The court also dismissed a separate appeal concerning the district court's refusal to allow additional material and appoint legal counsel. It found that this decision was not among the types of orders that could be appealed at that stage.With all three appeals dismissed, Ehn's emergency request to suspend the property sale no longer had a pending appeal to support it. articles.title: Beatles venue may not be allowed to play live music on rooftop
articles.summary: The proposed museum on Savile Row may get the greenlight on Tuesday but is facing objections.
articles.body:
Plans to create a museum where The Beatles performed their last live performance is expected to be approved - but on condition no live music can be played on the rooftop that made the Mayfair venue famous.

Apple Corps Ltd, the company founded by the band, wants to convert 3 Savile Row into a seven-floor "cultural experience and exhibition" celebrating The Beatles, with a basement café-bar on the site of the studio where Let It Be was recorded in 1969.

The Beatles famously stunned locals in January 1969 by playing a set on the roof of the Grade II* listed building, which was Apple Corps' headquarters.

Westminster City councillors are due to vote on the plans on Tuesday.

The council papers set out for the first time the scale of the attraction Sir Paul McCartney announced in May .

Apple Corps is forecasting up to 900 visitors each weekday and 1,140 on weekends, entering in timed slots of 20 people every 10 minutes.

There is a proposed limit of 225 visitors at any one time.

The basement café/bar would open until midnight seven nights a week, and events would be capped at 104 a year, averaging two events a week.

The draft conditions also state that no live music can be played on the terrace and any amplified music or speech should be noise limited. A two-metre-high acoustic barrier has also been proposed.

The Savile Row Bespoke Association, which represents the street's bespoke tailors, has objected to the plans stating they are in conflict with the Savile Row Special Policy Area planning designation that aims to protect bespoke tailoring on the street.

It has also warned that narrow pavements "would lead to dangerous congestion and have a significant negative impact on those who visit and work on Savile Row".

The Mayfair Neighbourhood Forum has not objected in principle but said visitor numbers "need to be greatly reduced" and asked for the operation to be monitored for 12 months before any expansion.

Planning officers state "the proposal does not comply wholly" with the Special Policy Area but say the building's unique link to The Beatles justifies an exception.

They have suggested a clause that would require the building to revert to its previous office or retail use if the venue closed.

Announcing the plans in May, Sir Paul told the BBC that tourists "come to England and they can go to Abbey Road, but they can't go inside" and described the Savile Row project as "a terrific idea".

He said visitors would "work your way up through the building… until you get to the top, where you go out on the roof and pretend to be a Beatle".

The Beatles at 3 Savile Row is due to open in 2027, if planning permission is obtained.

articles.title: Inside the heated debate over Scotland's data centres
articles.summary: The BBC's Lorna Gordon finds out how data centres operate and hears arguments for and against them.
articles.body:
There is strict security in place as we enter what looks like a nondescript office building on the outskirts of Airdrie.

We are stepping into a facility at the centre of a heated debate about the growth in data centres in Scotland.

Opponents argue that centres like this one are of no benefit to the local community and damage the environment.

DataVita claims its operations in North Lanarkshire are providing jobs and securing "data sovereignty" in Scotland.

It's rare to get access to a data centre.

They can process sensitive or valuable data; the companies who run them like to stay in the background.

You have to pass through a series of security measures as you enter the facility at Chapelhall.

There are perimeter fences and CCTV outside the building, a large grey box with occasional flashes of blue and white.

Inside there are airlocked doors allowing one person in and out at a time, and timed entry to some of the rooms.

You need a pass to move around and visitors must have an escort at all times.

Data centres have a lot of processing power, located in what is known as a server hall.

As the door opens to this pristine white space the first thing that hits you is the noise - and then the heat.

Thousands turn out in Edinburgh to protest against AI data centres

Why are data centres such a big deal in Scotland?

Second data centre planned for Lanarkshire as regulations tightened

"People are often surprised how hot it is in here," says DataVita's chief executive Danny Quinn.

"You can actually feel it coming out of the rack and going through. We then use the lovely cool climate of Scotland to cool that air and recirculate it through the data centre."

Not all the aisles are as hot. In others, colder air is sucked up through the floor and into the equipment to make sure it doesn't overheat.

Quinn says there is a misconception that freezing cold locations would be ideal for data centres.

"What you want is the kind of 'beige' - between 9 and 13 degrees - that Scotland is very good at all year round," he says.

He adds that the rack of servers we have been looking at consume roughly the same amount of electricity as a four-bedroom home every day.

An AI rack would use energy equivalent of 20 to 30 homes, he says.

The processing power can be used for internet searches and to store bank and health records as well as data for multiple businesses and public bodies.

"Data centres are the most valuable commodity in business now," Quinn says.

"If a company loses its data, it predominantly loses its ability to operate.

"We have an obligation to keep their data secure, and to ensure that customers' most critical asset - data - always stays on."

DataVita is planning to scale up at Chapelhall.

The 16 megawatt centre is the largest in Scotland, while another 24 MW centre is currently under construction.

The company is also seeking planning permission for a 120 MW centre.

The sites would hold a mixture of conventional servers and those working with AI.

From the end of her street, Jennifer Thompson can see all the sites where DataVita hopes to build.

"Some of my neighbours have been here for years," she says.

"They want to move because of the centres."

Thompson is a member of the Say No to Chapelhall AI Growth Zone group.

She has concerns over the environmental impact, the number of jobs and energy use.

"There's no good environmental outcome. There's no good biodiversity outcome. There's no good jobs outcome. There's no good pollution control," she says.

Thompson says it's not just about her community.

"I'd be hard pressed to find a community anywhere on earth that says we're really glad we've got these," she says.

"I don't think data centres should be anywhere until they prove that they are safe."

Last weekend, members of the group were among thousands of people who took part in a demonstration in Edinburgh against the building of large-scale AI data centres.

DataVita say they have had four public consultations at Chapelhall and that only 15 of the 150 people who came to look around the site had negative comments.

Quinn says infrastructure is needed in Scotland for what he describes as an AI revolution, and that this will provide "data sovereignty".

"It's important not just for the economy but for cybersecurity and the physical security of the nation," he says.

"We need to make sure we have our own infrastructure that is independent of any other nation."

He says DataVita hires and pays taxes and rates in Scotland and that any benefits stay within the country.

There are more than 20 planning applications for AI data centres in Scotland.

Quinn says some of those are "speculative applications" in places that have caused people "genuine concern."

He refuses to be drawn on how many data centres might be spread across Scotland within the next 10 years.

"Anyone stargazing into the future about AI is a very brave person, and ultimately what we need to ensure is that Scotland has the right type of technology to support an evolving technology," he says.

The Scottish government is promising new planning guidelines for data centres before the end of the year.

Opponents say Scotland cannot cope, doesn't need, and won't benefit from large hyperscale sites.

Those who want to build them say this an opportunity the country cannot afford to miss.

articles.title: Water firm lifts lid on fats beneath Devon businesses
articles.summary: A water company asks food firms to stop pouring fats and oils down sinks and protect drains.
articles.body:
A water company is renewing appeals to businesses to dispose of cooking waste carefully after uncovering build ups of fats, oil and grease underneath food outlets.

South West Water found a "substantial grease build-up" at a flooded kebab shop in Exmouth and also large quantities of fats, oils and grease in drainage chambers at a Sidmouth cafe, which were restricting the flow of wastewater.

Adrian Robinson, sewer network protection team manager, said: "What happens beneath food businesses can have a real impact on the sewer network."

He said it was important to dispose of fats properly "to prevent blockages, reduce the risk of flooding and pollution, and protect the environment".

The discoveries followed visits to cafes, restaurants, takeaways and ice cream parlours over the summer to check their drainage systems and make improvements to avoid blockages.

Last year the company cleared more than 5,500 avoidable blockages from its network, many linked to fats, oil and grease, alongside items such as wet wipes and sanitary products entering the wastewater network after being flushed down loos, rather than being disposed of carefully.

Other discoveries during the summer visits included fats, oils and grease accumulating beneath an ice cream parlour in Exmouth despite grease management measures being in place.

They discovered grease building up underneath manholes serving a food business in Cranbrook, near Exeter.

They also found fats, oils and grease entering the drainage system in Exeter.

South West Water said businesses can take steps to avoid blockages, flooding and pollution incidents.

These include maintaining grease traps and improving waste disposal practices.

The company said fat, oil and grease solidifies when it is poured down sinks and gradually builds up inside pipes, restricting the flow of wastewater.

If it is combined with other items such as wet wipes that are flushed down toilets, fat, oils and grease can contribute to stubborn blockages known as fatbergs, which can lead to flooding and pollution.

South West Water said people can take steps to help by:

Avoiding pouring fats, oils or grease down sinks and drains

Scrape leftover food into the bin before washing up

Regularly maintain grease management equipment such as grease traps and interceptors

Dispose of food waste and cooking oils appropriately

Only flush the three Ps: pee, poo and paper

articles.title: Daisy Hill: Woman faces hour-long drive to give birth as hospital suspends maternity services
articles.summary: From Monday, maternity services at Daisy Hill Hospital will move to Craigavon Area Hospital.
articles.body:
A couple who are expecting their first child have said their excitement has turned "into complete worry" because of the suspension of maternity services at their local hospital.

Shelly Magee was due to give birth in Newry's Daisy Hill Hospital in County Armagh in January but from Monday, the Southern Trust is moving all hospital-based births to Craigavon, about 20 miles away.

Her partner, Clinton McKeever, said the journey from their home in Mullaghbawn could take them up to 90 minutes in bad weather or heavy traffic.

The Southern Health Trust apologised to families facing longer journeys but said the shortage of obstetricians meant services must be temporarily concentrated at one hospital.

"We mean it when we say it's temporary - we're going out to make further attempts to recruit," said its chief executive, Steve Spoerry.

From Monday, all expectant mothers who receive treatment from the trust have been advised to go to Craigavon Area Hospital - not Daisy Hill - for all labour and birthing services, inpatient maternity care and emergency gynaecology support.

It added that patients would receive the same high standard of care from experienced specialists, including staff from Daisy Hill who are relocating to Craigavon.

Woman says 40-mile journey to hospital while having contractions was 'scary'

Knock-on effects if maternity services suspended, trust chief says

'My son might not have survived without Daisy Hill maternity service'

But the expectant couple have not been reassured by the trust's statements.

Magee said Craigavon Area Hospital was "50 minutes from the house" by car.

"A child doesn't choose a time to come," McKeever told BBC News NI.

"To strip away a maternity service and claim it's for the safety of women is scandalous... there's no thought of safety in that journey."

He said he was speaking from experience, having "had a taste of the journey already in a scenario that would be considered a crisis".

About five years ago, his father suffered several broken ribs and a punctured lung in a fall.

McKeever drove his father to Craigavon, having been advised by their local health clinic that it would take too long for an ambulance to get to Mullaghbawn.

"The traffic was crazy and he felt every bump - I felt guilty for every bump. I got him there in the end but it was a very, very stressful journey," he recalled.

"To know that I have to do it again with Shelly here, it's very concerning. It's took the excitement out of the whole thing and turned it into complete worry."

To avoid having to drive to Craigavon in labour in January the couple are considering booking a hotel or rented accommodation near the hospital.

Despite their concerns, they praised their midwives in Newry and Crossmaglen, acknowledging staff also face uncertainty.

The trust's chief executive apologised for the temporary closure which was first announced in September , but insisted there was no choice.

"I'd like to say to Clinton and Shelly that I'm really sorry it has come to this," Spoerry told the BBC's Good Morning Ulster programme .

"We wanted to maintain services at both hospitals, but our priority has, as they would expect, to be the safety of women and babies.

"And the safest way to provide the service, given the shortage of obstetricians is to concentrate the clinical team on one hospital only for the delivery of babies."

Asked if the risks posed by longer travel times was taken in account, Spoerry said there was "always an increased risk if people have to travel further for any service".

But he added it would be more dangerous for pregnant women to arrive into an understaffed maternity unit.

However, campaigners from the Daisy Hill Future Group claimed longer journey times would put more pressure on ambulance services and subject families in counties Down, Armagh and the border area to "life and death risks".

"Moving up to 1,800 births from Newry to Craigavon risks not just destabilising Craigavon's maternity unit but will threaten also its ability to safely provide other acute medical services," said its chair, Conor Patterson

Daisy Hill lost its emergency general surgery service in 2024, two years after it had been temporarily moved to Craigavon due to recruitment challenges.

The campaign group said the "obsessive pursuit of service transfer" out of Daisy Hill has left Craigavon Area Hospital "severely overstretched".

Health Minister Robbie Butler said: "Every avenue was explored to keep the service at Daisy Hill - there was international recruitment attempts.

"I have to reinforce that it is and very much remains to be a temporary move and no stone will be left unturned to remedy that as soon as it can be done."

According to figures from the trust, 1,713 babies were born at Daisy Hill last year, while Craigavon dealt with 2,768 births.

When asked how Craigavon will deal with hundreds of extra births each year, the trust said it was continuing efforts to secure consultant obstetricians for Daisy Hill.

It added that an existing ward at Craigavon has been reconfigured to provide 17 beds to accommodate antenatal and gynaecology admissions.

The general medical beds previously in that ward have been relocated.

The trust spokesperson said that of the 1,088 planned Southern Trust births up to the end of February, it estimated that 294 of these were originally planned for Daisy Hill.

A proportion of these women may already have been referred to Craigavon based on risk.

The trust said an estimated 13 women could possibly deliver their babies in Craigavon on Monday - the first day of the new system.

That includes planned C sections and those booked in for induction - four of these had originally planned to have their babies in Daisy Hill.

The trust employs 15 consultant obstetricians. However, sickness, reduced working hours and maternity leave means not all 15 can contribute to the on-call rota.

The number of midwives employed within the maternity units at both acute hospitals has dropped from pre-pandemic levels.

In October 2019, there were 55.6 midwives employed on a full-time basis at Daisy Hill Hospital and 95.04 full-time in Craigavon.

As of last month, that had dropped to 47.57 midwives at Daisy Hill and 82.58 in Craigavon.

However, the trust said midwifery care has changed over the past seven years, with more midwives now working in the community.

The trust added that 16 newly-appointed midwives are due to start work between November 2026 and January 2027.

To support the maternity service at Craigavon, a total of 37 staff, including midwives and sisters, are to transfer from Daisy Hill.

articles.title: Eyesore or icon - should Leeds clock tower landmark stay or go?
articles.summary: The Yorkshire Post tower has been a Leeds mainstay for decades, but it could soon be gone.
articles.body:
The Yorkshire Post clock tower has been a Leeds landmark for as long as many people in the city can remember.

"I have just never known it not be there," says 56-year-old Jacquie Raistritk, who is the same age as the tower which has overlooked Wellington Street since 1970.

"It's a landmark, although it's fairly ugly."

But, whether you like it or loathe it, the clock and temperature gauge could soon be gone for good.

A planning application for site clearance and demolition has been submitted to Leeds City Council, with a view to building two new blocks housing offices and shops.

Urbanite Leeds Ltd, which is behind the application, secured planning permission in 2023 to turn the site into student flats but, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service , the scheme ran into complications.

While the tower would be demolished, the proposed design for the 15 and 17-storey buildings does feature "a contemporary interpretation of this important element of the site's heritage".

Urbanite said one option under consideration was a digital display of both the time and the temperature on different parts of the building's facade.

The design of the proposed offices also features nods to the heritage of the site, which housed a printing works and offices for the Yorkshire Post and the Yorkshire Evening Post for 42 years until 2012.

As we walk along Wellington Place on a drizzly and grey midweek afternoon, the tower is in a sad state.

Dirt from being exposed to the elements is clearly visible, while neither the clock nor temperature gauge is working.

Manual labourers Karl and Oliver survey the landmark as they wait for a bus on Wellington Street.

Karl's opinion, "to put it bluntly", cannot be printed due to his choice of words.

"Being from Leeds I would prefer to keep it, it's been there for years.

"Before mobile phones were about you would walk past and glance up at the time, it was a local timepiece."

"It would be like a sight," adds Oliver.

Jacquie is from Liversedge but still holds an emotional connection to the brutalist-inspired structure.

"It's a bit like the Shipley Clock Tower , it's horrible but I think it needs cleaning up and it needs to stay there."

Anthony Coates also agrees the tower, in its current state, "is a little bit of an eyesore".

But, like others we spoke to, he does not want to see it go.

"It would be nice if it was done up rather than someone taking it down," says the 38-year-old.

The Leeds Civic Trust is keen to see the tower retained as part of the new development.

Its director, Martin Hamilton, says: "Our feeling is, if at all possible, it should remain on site.

"To lose it completely would be a shame."

Labour MP Jon Trickett, a former Leeds City Council leader, agrees.

"Thousands of people pass it every single day. It was always there. It felt familiar.

"You can't stop progress but you have got to try to preserve things like that, which seems to me a symbol of that part of Leeds."

A Leeds City Council spokesperson said Urbanite was "considering options to improve the appearance of the tower" while the application is considered.

A decision is expected in the coming months.

articles.title: AI helps spot possible lung cancer, says Northamptonshire doctor
articles.summary: A doctor says an AI tool helps radiology teams but stresses it has not replaced clinical expertise.
articles.body:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is a "second pair of eyes" helping radiology teams identify possible cancer on chest X-rays, a specialist consultant has said.

At the general hospitals in Kettering and Northampton, AI software reviews patients' scans, highlighting subtle abnormalities that would be difficult to see otherwise.

Cornilius Mushambi, consultant radiographer, said it "increased confidence" in the final judgement made by a clinician, but stressed it did not replace human expertise.

With NHS England funding, the technology was introduced in November 2024 and has helped staff examine 62,661 chest X-rays.

The Kettering General Hospital NHS Foundation Trust (KGHFT) said once the AI tool had analysed the scan, the radiology team assessed whether the finding needed further investigation.

KGHFT said that could mean a possible lung cancer was investigated earlier and the scans that appeared most urgent could be prioritised for review.

Mushambi said: "It means potentially a patient can leave our hospital with both their X-ray and CT [a scan that creates detailed images of the body] completed and reported on by a radiographer.

"Without input from AI, these steps that might otherwise have taken place days apart," he added.

KGHFT says the AI scan reports are accessible to radiology staff, but there are discussions about the marked-up images being made available to other teams, including in the emergency department.

It is hoped it could help medical professionals see potentially serious findings sooner, particularly in out-of-hours care.

The trust said: "AI offers another layer of support for patient care.

"It does not replace clinical expertise: every X-ray still requires a clinician's assessment and final judgement.

"The aim is to help patients who need further investigation move to the next stage of their care sooner."

The government has said chest X-rays are one of the most important tools in diagnosing lung cancer, the UK's biggest cancer killer, accounting for about one in five cancer deaths.

About seven million chest X-rays are carried out across the NHS each year.

articles.title: Political ambush? Eisenkot plans surprise govt announcement in Israel, swift Knesset vote to thwart defections
articles.summary: Yashar party chairman Gadi Eisenkot is planning to announce a coalition government at an unexpected moment in the coming weeks and push for a Knesset vote
articles.body: Yashar party chairman Gadi Eisenkot is planning to announce a coalition government at an unexpected moment in the coming weeks and push for a Knesset vote within 24 to 48 hours to prevent political manoeuvres and defections. The development comes as efforts to replace PM Benjamin Netanyahu remain deadlocked.Despite limited progress towards agreements with ultra-Orthodox factions, Arab-led parties and Netanyahu’s Likud, Eisenkot has pledged to try to form a government. According to the Times of Israel, citing public broadcaster Kan, his strategy is to put potential coalition partners under pressure by leaving little time for them to reconsider their positions or defect.Eisenkot is reportedly banking on some lawmakers abstaining rather than voting against his government, potentially allowing him to take office at the head of a minority administration, even if it subsequently collapses and triggers fresh elections.The reported plan comes amid divisions within Eisenkot’s own political camp, with several members publicly rejecting possible coalition arrangements.On Sunday, Yashar and Likud resumed unity government negotiations in Herzliya. After four hours of discussions, the two parties issued a brief joint statement saying they had discussed “core issues” and would meet again, without announcing a date for the next round. Likud was represented by Knesset faction leader Ofir Katz and Netanyahu’s longtime attorney Michael Rabello.The renewed talks followed Eisenkot’s decision to invite Likud representatives for intensive negotiations in an attempt to form a broad-based government. Yashar described the initiative as a sincere effort to establish the widest possible government and said it would explore all avenues to break the political deadlock.However, Likud has demanded that Eisenkot’s bloc suspend its legislative agenda and end cooperation with Arab parties. Eisenkot has ruled out a rotation arrangement with Netanyahu, insisting that he would serve as the sole prime minister in any unity government.Meanwhile, Netanyahu reiterated his support for a national unity government. In a post on X on Monday, he said, “A national unity government is the only government that can meet the challenges we face. To do so, it must include all parties that regard the State of Israel as the state of the Jewish people.”He added, “In any government that is formed, we will work together with our Haredi partners and enshrine in law, by mutual agreement, the status of those who study Torah.”Separately, a bill proposed by Yisrael Beytenu lawmaker Oded Forer and members of Eisenkot’s bloc is expected to come up for a preliminary reading in the Knesset on Wednesday, Israel's Channel 12 reported. It seeks to limit prime ministerial tenure to eight years, prevent indicted politicians from forming governments and end a prime minister’s tenure if indicted for serious offences involving moral turpitude.The proposal is widely seen as targeting Netanyahu, who has faced a corruption trial for more than six years. However, Channel 12 said it may face constitutional hurdles and could primarily serve as leverage in coalition negotiations.President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with forming a government on November 8, giving him an initial 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension, to secure the support of at least 61 members in the 120-seat Knesset. The coming weeks will determine whether his surprise-vote strategy can break the deadlock.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In Andy Jassy vs Mark Zuckerberg 'fight' over AI agents, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella picks a 'favourite'
articles.summary: Satya Nadella sees an opening for AI shopping agents.
articles.body: Satya Nadella sees an opening for AI shopping agents. Speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit, the Microsoft CEO said retailers that turn away agents could send shoppers to rivals that let the software browse and buy on their behalf. The discussion with Andrew Ross Sorkin touched on Amazon’s advertising business and its decision to block Muse, the personal AI agent developed by Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta.“So if you don't accept the agent, somebody else will; if Amazon doesn't, Shop will,” Nadella said. He used “Shop” in the exchange, which can be a reference to Shopify; however, he didn't specify. It can be as Meta says Muse already has access to Shopify’s catalogue, and eligible Shopify merchants can even let shoppers check out directly in Microsoft Copilot. In September, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse AI agent, alleging that it accessed the site without permission or identifying itself as an AI agent, raising concerns about the security of customer accounts and login credentials.How Amazon and Meta want AI agents to shopMeta built Muse to carry out tasks across websites and apps. It runs in a dedicated virtual computer with its own browser, so it can visit sites on a user’s behalf. Meta says Muse asks for approval before making a purchase and shows users a record of its actions. The company has also announced plans to add Shop Pay and PayPal as payment options.Andy Jassy’s Amazon offers its own agent, Alexa for Shopping, on its website and app. It can compare products, track prices, build a cart and automate routine purchases. Shopify gives merchants another option through Copilot. They can let customers find eligible products and enter payment and shipping details in the chat, or direct shoppers to their own storefront to finish the purchase.Who gets paid when an AI agent shopsNadella compared the shift to the move from web portals like Yahoo to search engines. If an agent compares products and brings a shopper straight to checkout, the retailer has fewer opportunities to show that shopper ads. Nadella suggested that charging for clicks or transactions could become more important. “If you’re in love with a particular business model, you have to kind of scramble,” he said.Nadella also raised a question about how the systems would work together. He expects people to delegate tasks to agents and those agents to use shared systems to conduct commerce. The retailer still has to decide whether to accept an agent acting for a customer. “And where does the liability go?” he asked.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Rotterdam built a public square that turns into a giant rainwater reservoir during heavy downpours; when the weather is dry, its basins become basketball and volleyball courts
articles.summary: Rotterdam has found a unique way to deal with heavy rainfall by turning a public square into a temporary water storage space that also serves as a
articles.body: Rotterdam has found a unique way to deal with heavy rainfall by turning a public square into a temporary water storage space that also serves as a recreational area. The Water Square Benthemplein, designed by Dutch architecture firm De Urbanisten, collects rainwater during downpours and holds it in specially designed basins. During the dry season, the same area becomes a place for residents to play basketball, volleyball and other sports, demonstrating how urban infrastructure can serve more than one purpose.How Rotterdam's water square stores rainwater during heavy downpoursThe Water Square Benthemplein was created to address a problem that Rotterdam has faced during intense rainfall. When large amounts of rain fall within a short period, parts of the city can flood because the existing water system cannot always process the additional water quickly enough.The Climate Adaptation Platform Netherlands says that the concept of water squares is to give residential areas places where rainwater can be collected and released in a controlled way. Instead of letting too much water overwhelm the drainage system, specially designed public spaces temporarily hold the water until the city’s water infrastructure can handle it.Benthemplein is one of the most prominent examples of this approach. The square has a storage capacity of 1,800 cubic metres, making it a significant part of Rotterdam's efforts to manage heavy rainfall. Its design also ensures that the space remains useful to residents when there is no immediate need to store water.The project was designed by De Urbanisten and officially opened on 4 December 2013, according to Landezine's project profile.Three basins manage different levels of rainfallOne of the most important features of Benthemplein is its 3 separate water basins. According to the Dutch Architects, 2 shallow basins collect rainwater from the immediate surroundings whenever it rains. A third, deeper basin is designed to receive water when rainfall continues for longer and larger quantities need to be stored.The water reaches these basins through large stainless-steel gutters that run across the square. The design also includes a water wall and a rain well, which make the movement of rainwater visible to people visiting the space. The water wall directs rainfall towards the deeper basin, while the rain well brings water from a neighbouring building into the gutter system.De Urbanisten explains that the water is gradually channelled into the square rather than being allowed to collect unpredictably. The design also accounts for what happens after the rain stops. According to Dutch Architects, water collected in the shallow basins moves into an underground infiltration system, allowing it to gradually seep into the groundwater. This helps maintain groundwater levels and supports nearby trees and plants, particularly during dry periods.Water from the deeper basin is returned to Rotterdam's open-water system within a maximum of 36 hours. This arrangement also prevents all the collected rainwater from immediately entering the city's combined sewage system.The square is also useful when there is no rainThe water square was never intended to function only as a flood-control facility. Its designers wanted to create a lively neighbourhood destination that residents could enjoy throughout the year.When the basins are dry, the deeper section becomes a sports area where visitors can play basketball, football and volleyball. The stepped edges around the basin also provide seating, allowing spectators to watch games or simply spend time with others.The shallower sections have different recreational uses. One is designed for skating and other activities on wheels, while another includes a smooth surface intended for dancing and informal gatherings. The surrounding areas feature trees, ornamental grasses and flowers, creating quieter places for people who prefer to sit and relax.Landezine's project description highlights how the square combines sports facilities, greenery and water management without making the recreational areas feel like secondary additions. The design uses different shades of blue on surfaces that can hold water, while stainless steel marks the structures that transport it. This makes the square's water-management purpose visible even during dry weather.Local residents helped shape the designAccording to Dutch Architects, students and teachers from Zadkine College and the Graphic Lyceum, members of a nearby church, a youth theatre, a gym and local residents participated in the planning process.Three workshops were organised to discuss how the square should look, what activities it should accommodate and how rainwater could become part of the experience. Participants wanted a place that offered plenty of room for young people while also providing green and quieter areas for relaxation.The German Development Institute's 2021 paper explains that the consultation process took place over 6 months and focused on activities, design choices and refining the ideas proposed by participants. The paper notes that the workshops shaped features such as the basketball area, skating facilities and seating arrangements.Rotterdam has expanded the water square conceptBenthemplein is not the only public space of its kind in Rotterdam. The city has developed smaller water squares in other neighbourhoods as part of its wider approach to managing rainfall.According to the Climate Adaptation Platform Netherlands, Bellamy Square in Spangen includes a water-storage section with a capacity of 250 cubic metres. Another example is Kleinpolder Square in Overschie, where an underground basin collects overflow water from nearby surface water. The space also accommodates public sculptures placed on raised platforms to protect them from flooding.Benthemplein’s large storage capacity also made the construction more expensive. Piling work was required during construction, while funding included support from the Dutch government's Beautiful Netherlands Innovation Programme and an INTERREG subsidy from the European Union.De Urbanisten's research into water squares began in 2006-2007, and the concept became part of Rotterdam's official urban policy through Rotterdam Waterplan 2 in 2007.You use AI every day. articles.title: Amtrak train derails after striking 18-wheeler at Louisiana crossing
articles.summary: An Amtrak train struck a semi-trailer truck in Louisiana, causing several cars to derail and sending a few passengers to to the hospital.
articles.body:
Nov. 23 (UPI) -- An Amtrak train struck a semi-trailer truck hauling a bulldozer Sunday evening in a suburb of Lafayette, La., causing several train cars to derail and sending several passengers to the hospital, authorities said.

The Lafayette Police Department was notified of the crash in the 100 block of Thruway Park Road in Broussard at about 6:05 p.m. CST, Sgt. Ashley Wood told reporters at a Sunday night press conference .

She said the train crashed into the 18-wheeler as it was crossing the tracks at a controlled rail road crossing.

Injuries reported to police have so far been minor, she said, adding that "a few" passengers have been transported to the hospital. The Lafayette Fire Department later said five minor injuries were reported. Acadian Ambulance, which deployed 12 ambulances to the crash, said in a statement that it had transported four patients with non-life-threatening injuries.

According to the fire department, several cars derailed.

There were 95 passengers, according to fire officials.

"Hazmat and rescue personnel ensured the scene was safe for first responders to assist the injured and check on the other passengers," the Lafayette Fire Department said in a post to Facebook.

"Once it was safe for passengers to exit, firefighters assisted them to a safe location along with their luggage."

articles.title: 'She will have to face music': Bangladesh reaffirms Sheikh Hasina will be arrested if she returns
articles.summary: As Sheikh Hasina’s self-announced December deadline to return from India approaches, Dhaka has reaffirmed that the former prime minister will be arrested
articles.body: As Sheikh Hasina’s self-announced December deadline to return from India approaches, Dhaka has reaffirmed that the former prime minister will be arrested if she returns to Bangladesh.Shama Obaed, Bangladesh’s state minister for foreign affairs, also called on New Delhi to "honour" its extradition treaty with Dhaka."As soon as she (Hasina) tries to enter Bangladesh, she will be arrested and taken to jail, and the law will take its course," Obaed told Reuters on Sunday."We would like India to honour the extradition treaty and return her as a convict. The law will take its course. She will have to face the music," the minister added.Sheikh Hasina, the daughter of Bangladesh's founding father Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, has been living in New Delhi since August 5, 2024, when she resigned and fled the country following a student-led uprising that brought down her Awami League government. The United Nations estimates that up to 1,400 people were killed during the unrest.The former PM was tried in absentia and convicted of crimes against humanity linked to the July Uprising, as the movement is known in Bangladesh. She has dismissed the verdict as an act of political vendetta.In August, Sheikh Hasina announced plans to return to Bangladesh by December. She has since applied for a new passport and identity card, but the Bangladesh Nationalist Party-led government has turned down both requests.Also Read | 'I'd rather die in Bangladesh': Hasina's defiant message on returning to DhakaThe standoff has prompted Awami League supporters to take to the streets. The party, which was banned by the interim administration of Muhammad Yunus, announced nationwide protests and rallies this month in support of its leader.Over the past 10 days, police have recorded dozens of crude bomb blasts and arson attacks targeting vehicles across at least 28 districts, leaving several police officers and civilians injured, local media reported.Also Read | 'Conspiring to keep their masters happy': Bangladesh PM blames Sheikh Hasina for fresh arson attacksObaed described the violence as a survival tactic by Sheikh Hasina's "politically bankrupt political party."The foreign affairs minister also responded to a report that India had set conditions for extraditing Sheikh Hasina."There have been no official discussions with India about sending an aircraft to bring Hasina back. … We want balanced ties that do not compromise Bangladesh's 'dignity, self-respect and interests'," she added.New Delhi has repeatedly maintained that Dhaka's request for Sheikh Hasina's extradition remains under consideration.You use AI every day. articles.title: South East Water reports loss after penalties and supply failures
articles.summary: South East Water records a pre-tax loss of £22.9m in the six months to 30 September.
articles.body:
South East Water has reported a half-year loss after penalties and £29m of costs following disruption to water supplies over the summer.

The company, which serves about 2.4 million customers across south-east England, recorded a pre-tax loss of £22.9m in the six months to 30 September, compared with a profit of £18.2m during the same period last year.

In July, regulator Ofwat ordered the company to spend £30.5m on improvements after supply interruptions hit customers across Kent and Sussex which affected more than 286,000 customers.

The company spent £29m responding to further supply interruptions during summer heatwaves in Kent and Sussex .

This included providing bottled water, setting up emergency water stations and compensating customers.

South East Water said it had set aside £14.6m in its latest financial results to cover the redress package.

The company supplies water to customers in Kent, East and West Sussex, Surrey, Hampshire and Berkshire.

Hosepipe bans remain in force across all areas supplied by South East Water.

In October, it was forced to ask shareholders for £50m after warning earlier in the year that it required additional funding in order to stay afloat.

The company said there were "early signs of improvement" following changes to its leadership team and plans for a "significant transformation" of the business.

Earlier this year, John Halsall was appointed chief executive after former chief executive David Hinton and chair Chris Train stepped down .

The departures followed criticism from MPs who said they had "no confidence" in the company's leadership after a review of repeated supply outages.

Richard Morse is due to become chair of the company on 3 December, succeeding interim chair Lisa Clement.

South East Water said the initial signs were "encouraging", although it warned improvements would take time to become fully visible to customers.

A spokesperson for the company said: "We know that customers will not judge us on the number of initiatives we launch or the promises we make.

"They will judge us on whether their water supply is more reliable, whether we communicate better and whether we provide the right support when they need it – we look forward to providing the evidence in future results."

articles.title: Nvidia chip scandal: How deep are Alice Huang, her 'husband' entangled in China's spy web?
articles.summary: Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman at the centre of the Nvidia chip-smuggling scandal, allegedly maintained contact with a Chinese intelligence
articles.body: Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman at the centre of the Nvidia chip-smuggling scandal, allegedly maintained contact with a Chinese intelligence officer for more than a year — during a period that overlapped with her reported relationship with Nvidia’s former chief executive Jensen Huang.Alice, also known as Huang Le, was in contact with an official of China’s Ministry of State Security (MSS) from spring 2025 to autumn 2026, according to a New York Times report. US intelligence agencies have also gathered evidence suggesting that her business partner, Kang Wei, often introduced as her husband, worked with the same agency.The revelations deepen scrutiny of a network of Southeast Asian companies suspected of acquiring advanced Nvidia chips and supplying computing power to Chinese firms, with some servers allegedly diverted to China in breach of US export controls.Corporate records and research by intelligence firm Strider Technologies reviewed by the Times also point to links between Alice’s family and associates, Nvidia partners, data centres and Chinese state-owned defence contractors, including businesses connected to the People’s Liberation Army.The extent of Alice and Kang’s alleged intelligence work remains under investigation.The alleged spy links: Alice Huang and Kang WeiAccording to NYT, US intelligence agencies monitored Alice Huang’s contacts with the MSS for more than a year, including during the period when she was involved with Jensen Huang.The newspaper reported that US intelligence had gathered evidence of Kang Wei’s work with the same agency. Alice also appears to have met officials from China’s Ministry of Public Security, the country’s main law enforcement agency.The timing of the alleged contacts has become a focus of US officials because it overlaps with the period when Alice’s company, Megaspeed, was acquiring large quantities of Nvidia chips.The company’s hardware was used to provide computing capacity to data centres in Southeast Asia serving Chinese technology companies, including Alibaba. Some of the servers are suspected of having been transferred to China.NYT said the intelligence contained evidence, including shipping records, demonstrating Alice and Kang’s roles in a network of companies involved in the procurement and movement of Nvidia chips.US officials are still working to establish the full extent and duration of their alleged work with Chinese intelligence. The nature of Alice’s ties to the MSS and the extent to which her network supplied chips or computing power to Chinese military projects remain under investigation.The Chinese embassy has denied allegations that Alice was a spy.How Alice Huang entered Nvidia’s business networkAlice’s connection to Jensen Huang reportedly began years before the current scandal.According to media outlet The Information, Alice was introduced to Jensen through Kang, who had business dealings with the Nvidia chief in the 2010s while acquiring Chinese video game companies.Chinese media reports and social media posts have claimed that Kang would highlight his wife’s association with Jensen to clients, while Alice regularly shared photographs with the Nvidia chief on her WeChat account. Her proximity to the Nvidia executive was reportedly an important factor in her business dealings in China.Alice later became a senior executive and equity partner at Shanghai Hexi Investment before joining Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre company that conducted substantial business involving Nvidia chips.She reportedly had no prior experience in the artificial intelligence sector before 2023, when Megaspeed was established.The New York Times reported that Alice’s family and associates had developed a network of companies connecting official Nvidia partners to state- and military-linked projects in China.Megaspeed, Kang Wei and the alleged chip-smuggling routeMegaspeed became central to the investigation into the alleged diversion of Nvidia chips. According to The Wall Street Journal, Alice Huang, her business partner Kang Wei and Chinese national Li Ming had worked together for years before Singapore prosecutors charged Li and others in February 2025 over the alleged transshipment of Nvidia-powered servers.Li was reportedly closely involved in Megaspeed’s operations. Prosecutors alleged he misled an American supplier about the servers’ destination, claiming they were for his Singapore company before the equipment was shipped to Malaysia and allegedly sent elsewhere.Alice and Kang had established a cloud-computing venture in 2021. Their network later acquired Megaspeed, which joined Nvidia’s cloud partner programme in November 2023 after identifying Alibaba as an anchor customer.While Megaspeed supplied offshore computing capacity to Alibaba, some servers were allegedly transferred to a Chinese company in breach of US export controls, the WSJ reported.Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its internal “no sell” list in June 2025. The company has denied wrongdoing and said Alice left in August. Singapore officials reportedly questioned her over suspected chip smuggling before allowing her to leave and barring her from re-entry.Culper Research separately claimed around 50,000 Nvidia chips were unaccounted for in a Megaspeed audit. The company has denied wrongdoing.The family’s links to China’s defence industryThe investigation has also turned to Alice’s family, particularly her sister Huang Yu, whose business interests intersect with China’s defence sector.A confidential analysis by Strider Technologies, reviewed by NYT, found that about $3.6 billion in Chinese government money flowed through companies associated with Alice’s family and business associates.The links stretch from data centres running Nvidia-powered servers to Chinese state-owned defence contractors. One of the most significant runs through Shanghai-based Century Litong, a cloud-computing company founded in 2023 by Century Longteng, in which Alice’s sister had an investment through a related firm.Century Litong was later acquired by Jiangsu Lettall Electronic, which also owns Nanjing Jinning Microwave, a manufacturer of components used in Chinese radar and missile systems, according to company disclosures and Strider’s research.The company has also leased Nvidia-powered servers at a Shanghai supercomputing centre through an affiliate of the Aviation Industry Corporation of China (AVIC), the state-owned aerospace and defence giant. Other business links connect the network to China Electronics Technology Group, a military-electronics conglomerate.The connections are often indirect, and the research does not establish that the PLA used computing power from data centres linked to Alice’s family.“Follow the money and, too often, you find the PLA at the end of it,” Strider chief executive Greg Levesque told NYT.Other names on the list included military-linked Zhejiang Lab and its co-founder, Alibaba.The Information had earlier reported links between Alice’s network and DeepSeek.The network did not stop with MegaspeedMegaspeed’s operations in Singapore largely went dormant after Alice’s departure, but people familiar with the business told the WSJ that members of the team were running a new venture, Novagate Cloud.Established in 2025, Novagate describes itself as an Nvidia cloud partner and says it operates at least two data centres equipped with the company’s advanced Blackwell chips.WSJ also identified corporate links between Novagate and companies associated with Century Litong.A May report by short-selling firm Culper Research suggested Novagate was likely linked to Megaspeed, citing similarities between their websites and the fact that one of Novagate’s directors shared an address with Megaspeed’s headquarters.The links have raised questions about whether the network that supplied computing capacity to Chinese customers continued to operate through new companies after Megaspeed came under scrutiny.China’s spy agency and the race for AI chipsThe alleged intelligence contacts have drawn attention because of the MSS’s expanding role in China’s effort to acquire advanced technology and overcome US export restrictions.For decades, the MSS has described its mission as countering espionage and political threats to Communist Party rule. But in April, China’s minister of state security, Chen Yixin, announced a sixth mission focused on overcoming technology “blockades” and advancing artificial intelligence.Matt Pottinger, who served as deputy national security adviser during Donald Trump’s first term and is now chief executive of research firm Garnaut Global, said the network of companies procuring and allegedly smuggling Nvidia chips aligned with the MSS’s stated mission.The intelligence about Alice was closely held within the US government until NYT reported its existence in late October.Before the scandal became public, advisers to Trump told him on at least two occasions that US intelligence had uncovered Alice’s alleged links to Chinese intelligence and that she was in a close relationship with Jensen Huang while he was still running Nvidia, according to US officials with direct knowledge of the briefings.On both occasions, Trump downplayed the concerns and made clear he did not want to intervene, the officials said. They said the president viewed Jensen Huang as a valuable ally and Nvidia as important to the US economy and stock market.Trump has since urged Nvidia’s board to consider bringing Jensen Huang back as chief executive, calling his departure a “tragedy” and describing him as a “brilliant man”.The president has also questioned whether Alice was a spy, saying: “Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy.”Jensen Huang’s resignation and the unanswered questionsJensen Huang initially described his interactions with Alice as normal business dealings with a customer. He acknowledged an affair only after NYT reported that Alice had been identified by US officials as a Chinese intelligence asset and that the Nvidia chief had been picked up on electronic surveillance targeting her.He resigned as Nvidia chief executive on November 12 after reports also emerged of an affair with a subordinate at the company. Nvidia’s board unanimously accepted his resignation and appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO. The board has rejected Trump’s suggestion that Jensen Huang be reinstated.Meanwhile, US intelligence agencies continue to investigate Alice, Kang and the network of companies associated with them.The investigation is far from over. US intelligence agencies are still trying to establish whether restricted Nvidia chips were diverted to China, how much computing power reached military-linked customers and what role Alice, Kang and their associates played in the alleged operation.At the centre of it all is a network that brought together Nvidia’s most advanced technology, Chinese intelligence and businesses linked to the country’s defence industry.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Children must learn distraction-free': Denmark to propose phone ban in schools in 2027
articles.summary: Denmark will propose a ban on mobile phones and other private internet-enabled devices in primary and lower secondary schools from the 2027 academic year.
articles.body: Denmark will propose a ban on mobile phones and other private internet-enabled devices in primary and lower secondary schools from the 2027 academic year. The country's education ministry announced the proposal on Monday, citing concerns over distractions caused by social media, online shopping and gaming. The plan also includes filtering school networks to block non-educational websites during lessons."Children should be able to go to school without constantly being distracted by things like social media, online shopping, and gaming," news agency Reuters quoted education minister Magnus Heunicke saying in a statement.The proposed restrictions will cover not just smartphones but also other privately owned electronic devices with internet access. Schools will introduce content filters to block websites considered to have no educational or pedagogical relevance during class hours.These will include social media platforms, gaming websites and online shopping sites. However, individual municipalities and schools will decide which specific websites should be blocked.Denmark's proposal comes amid growing efforts by countries to restrict smartphone use in schools over concerns about its impact on students' concentration and behaviour.The Netherlands, South Korea and Italy have already introduced bans on smartphones in schools. Poland and the Czech Republic proposed similar restrictions in June.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: An American artist has spent over two decades chasing America's biggest roadside attractions, from giant statues to oversized landmarks; she recreates nearly 200 of them as tiny models, some less than 2 inches tall, which are housed in a Kansas museum
articles.summary: For more than two decades, American artist Erika Nelson has travelled across the United States documenting some of its most unusual roadside attractions,
articles.body: For more than two decades, American artist Erika Nelson has travelled across the United States documenting some of its most unusual roadside attractions, from oversized sculptures to landmarks built to catch the attention of passing motorists. But instead of simply photographing these giant creations, Nelson recreates them as tiny handmade models, preserving the details and distinctive character of the original structures. Her growing collection, titled The World's Largest Collection of the World's Smallest Versions of the World's Largest Things, has earned recognition from Guinness World Records. Nearly 200 miniatures are now part of the collection, which has a permanent home at a dedicated exhibition space in Lucas, Kansas.How an artist began chasing America's biggest roadside attractionsNelson's fascination with oversized roadside landmarks dates back to her childhood. Growing up in Missouri, she remembers using a water tower painted to resemble a giant eight-ball as a local landmark. Visits to her grandparents in Minnesota also brought her face to face with the enormous Paul Bunyan statue, another attraction that stayed with her.The idea for her miniature collection took shape while she was studying art. During road trips, she began visiting unusual roadside structures, recording their stories and looking for souvenirs that captured what made each attraction special. When she could not find suitable keepsakes, she decided to make her own. She began with small replicas of the landmarks she encountered, gradually turning the idea into a long-running project.From a travelling museum to a permanent homeNelson spent two years living in a vehicle while exploring the United States, visiting roadside attractions and collecting stories about the people and communities behind them. As her collection grew, she converted a small bus into a mobile exhibition, taking the miniatures to art events, cultural centres, colleges and festivals.The travelling display eventually found a permanent home in downtown Lucas, Kansas. Nelson established the Roadside Sideshow Expo in 2017, turning an old storefront into a museum dedicated to her miniature interpretations of America's oversized landmarks. The exhibition brings together models from across the country, allowing visitors to explore the attractions without having to travel hundreds of miles between them.How she recreates giant landmarks in miniatureThe models are handmade, and Nelson selects materials according to the object she is recreating. For many attractions originally built from fibreglass or concrete, she uses two-part polymer clay or sculpting medium, followed by paint and other finishing details. She also adapts everyday objects when they can help reproduce a landmark's shape.Some of her material choices are particularly unusual. To recreate the world's largest ball of rubber bands, she used the tiny rubber bands commonly used by orthodontists. For a miniature version of the world's largest cow hairball, she used cat hair. Her replica of the giant baseball bat outside the Louisville Slugger Museum in Kentucky was made using a modified ornament and a model railway building adapted to resemble the museum.The stories behind the giant roadside attractionsFor Nelson, these structures are more than oversized objects designed to attract attention. Many are expressions of local identity, created by residents, businesses or communities hoping to give travellers a reason to stop and explore their towns. Their subjects range from familiar objects to unusual local symbols, with each attraction carrying a story about the place where it stands.One example that caught Nelson's attention was a giant concrete penny weighing around 17,000 pounds. Its story reflects the community spirit behind some of America's roadside creations. Other attractions represented in her collection include Otto the Otter, a giant baseball bat and an oversized rendering of Van Gogh's Three Sunflowers in a Vase in Goodland, Kansas.Nearly 200 miniatures earn Guinness World Records recognitionThe collection has received a Guinness World Records title for the largest collection of miniature replicas of the world's largest things. According to Guinness, the museum in Lucas contained around 200 handmade replicas as of 2025. Nelson's models are generally less than two inches in their largest dimension, making the contrast with the original attractions particularly striking.The collection continues to evolve as Nelson discovers more roadside landmarks and adds new pieces. The miniatures are intended as one-of-a-kind works rather than mass-produced souvenirs, and they are not generally offered for sale. Some have also been damaged by sunlight, temperature changes or visitors, while others have had to be retired after the original attractions were dismantled. The exhibition even has a display dedicated to models that have met unusual ends, preserving the stories of the miniatures that could not survive the journey.You use AI every day. articles.title: Indonesia seizes Bangladesh-bound cargo ship carrying chemicals from China that could make 100 missiles
articles.summary: The Indonesian Navy has seized a Comoros-flagged cargo vessel carrying 405 tonnes of sodium perchlorate, a powerful oxidising chemical used in industrial
articles.body: The Indonesian Navy has seized a Comoros-flagged cargo vessel carrying 405 tonnes of sodium perchlorate, a powerful oxidising chemical used in industrial processes and the manufacture of rocket propellants and certain explosives, in waters off Belawan.The vessel, MV Star Line, was travelling from China to Bangladesh when it was detained on November 7. Indonesian news outlet Waspada.id reported that the ship had stopped in Belawan waters to refuel before naval personnel noticed unusual movements and decided to inspect it.Rear Admiral Denny Septiana, commander of Indonesian Navy Regional Command I (Koarmada I), disclosed details of the seizure at a press conference in Belawan on November 20, according to The Dhaka Tribune.The navy's patrol vessel KRI Sigalu-857 reportedly became suspicious after detecting that the ship was operating outside its designated route. The patrol team contacted the vessel for further inspection, and subsequent checks revealed inconsistencies in its documents and cargo.The commander of KRI Sigalu, in coordination with Koarmada I headquarters, then ordered a search.Sodium perchlorate found in 15 containersAccording to the Indonesian Navy, the vessel was carrying 36 containers, of which 15 contained sodium perchlorate. The total quantity seized was 405 tonnes.The chemical is a strategic oxidising agent with industrial applications and is also used in the production of rocket and missile propellants.Rear Admiral Deny Septian said the seized quantity could potentially be used to manufacture up to 100 missiles.The same report said naval personnel also found 54 pallets containing millions of unregistered blank 4G LTE SIM cards aboard the vessel.The ship was reportedly travelling from Lianyungang Port in China to Mongla Port in Bangladesh. According to The Business Standard, it had been scheduled to arrive at Mongla at noon on November 8, but made an unscheduled stop in Indonesian waters.The identity of the importer of the cargo has not been established. Identifying the importer would require further investigation, as the vessel was intercepted before reaching Bangladesh and its Import General Manifest would ordinarily contain details of the importers and the goods being carried.Indonesian Navy examines vessel's documentsThe Indonesian Navy also found discrepancies in the vessel's registration documents.As per the report, the documents listed its International Maritime Organization (IMO) number as 8356962, official number as 1902384 and call sign as D-6A4384.Although the documents stated that they were valid until October 8, 2027, their validity status was listed as suspended.The vessel had a suspended registration status and potentially falsified shipping documents. It also said the ship allegedly failed to respond to radio communications.Denny Septiana said authorities were examining the vessel's administrative records, the validity of its navigation permits and whether it had complied with regulations governing the transportation of dangerous goods.Investigations and questioning of those aboard the vessel were underway to identify the people involved in the shipment.The Indonesian Navy had not disclosed the identities of the shipping company, cargo owners or intended recipients of the seized goods.What is sodium perchlorate?Sodium perchlorate (NaClO₄) is a strong oxidising chemical used in industrial and laboratory applications, as well as in the manufacture of rocket propellants, explosives and pyrotechnic products.It is not itself an explosive or a fuel, but can support combustion under certain conditions. Large quantities require careful handling because of potential fire and explosion hazards.The seizure has left questions about the ownership, origin and intended recipients of the 405-tonne consignment destined for Bangladesh.You use AI every day. articles.title: Cockerel dumping rises despite council allotment ban U-turn
articles.summary: Durham County Council has reversed a cockerel allotment ban but the birds are still being dumped.
articles.body:
Cockerel dumping has increased despite a council overturning its decision to ban the birds from allotments, a rescuer said.

Founder of Darlington Bird Rescue Laura Hewitt said the number of abandoned cockerels had increased "exponentially" since Durham County Council banned the birds on its allotments in March and gave owners 12 months to adhere to the rule.

Despite the ban U-turn, the birds continue to be dumped and Hewitt estimated she had been called out to rescue more than 50 birds this year including 22 abandoned on one occasion.

The council's neighbourhood protection manager Ian Hoult said it reversed the ban "following consultation with the public".

Cockerels were already banned on allotments due to noise nuisance, and changes made in March meant any remaining exceptions to the rule were removed.

The local authority back-tracked on the ban in September and said no enforcement action was taken while it was in place, and show cockerels were allowed on its allotments again.

However, Hewitt said cockerels were still being dumped.

"People don't want to, especially when it's birds they've raised, end up culling their own birds," Hewitt said.

Hewitt says Darlington Bird Rescue volunteers were still being called out to dumped birds on a weekly basis.

Once they are caught, volunteers look to rehome them, but this is difficult as chicken keepers tend to have one rooster to several hens.

"Compared to last year, I probably went out about five or six times," Hewitt said.

"Within about two months (of the ban), we had 20 different dumps, it was just one after another."

Hewitt criticised the local authority's approach in the weeks leading up to the ban.

"They weren't telling people what to do with them, they were just telling them to get rid," she said.

Irresponsible breeding and hatching projects also led to the birds being dumped, Hewitt said.

Hoult said: "Following consultation with the public, we reviewed our allotment policy, and a decision to overturn the ban was made on 16 September.

"No enforcement was carried out while the ban was in place as there was a one-year transition period for allotment holders to adjust to the ban."
